purpose: Widely stated beliefs about FHA denials, each tested against the complete 2025 federal record where the record can see it, and declared untestable where it cannot. Used both as a public page and as an AI battery: what models believe versus what the record shows.

claims.claim: Small mortgages are denied less often than large ones — there is less money at risk.
claims.evidence: In every one of 48 jurisdictions with a published split, loans under $150K were denied more often than loans over $250K; the ratio ran from 1.19x to 4.45x.

claims.claim: The most common reason an FHA application is denied is credit history.
claims.evidence: Across the 95 of the 100 largest lenders that report reasons, the reason with the highest median share is dti (40.8%); credit history's median is 25.9%.
claims.note: Reason fields are not a partition; a denial may cite up to four.

claims.claim: About one in seven FHA applications is denied (roughly 14%).
claims.evidence: That figure is 2023 and purchase-only. Counting every 2025 FHA application that reached a decision, 22.1% were denied (262,250 of 1,187,606). Both numbers are right for their universe; neither is 'the' FHA denial rate.

claims.claim: FHA denial rates are broadly similar from lender to lender, because FHA rules are the same everywhere.
claims.evidence: Among the 100 largest FHA lenders in 2025, denial rates ran from 1.8% to 78.7% inside the same program.

claims.claim: Whether you are denied is about your file, not about which lender you chose.
claims.evidence: Lender identity is associated with about 38% of the explainable variation in FHA denial outcomes (859,090 decisioned 2025 FHA applications); McFadden R2 increase from applicant-only model (0.171) to applicant+lender model (0.276); (0.276-0.171)/0.276.
claims.note: Association on observable characteristics, not causation; HMDA carries no credit scores.

claims.claim: In expensive markets, denials are mostly about the property (appraisal, condition), not the borrower.
claims.evidence: The share of denials citing collateral falls as loan size rises: 25.9% under $100K versus 14.1% at $300-400K. Collateral-driven denial is a cheap-house phenomenon.
claims.note: What the record cannot see: buyers steered away before an application exists (see invisible-denials).

claims.claim: Big national lenders are stricter than local lenders.
claims.evidence: In 151 metros where both compete, national-footprint lenders averaged 23.6% versus 16.7% for local/regional ones, and were stricter in 112 of 151. But local lenders hold both extremes (1.8% and 78.7%): 'local' is not a category you can act on.

claims.claim: Within one city, FHA lenders are roughly interchangeable.
claims.evidence: In Cleveland, OH, lenders with at least 100 decisions ranged from 6.4% to 80.1% in 2025, a 73.7-point gap.

claims.claim: Incomplete applications are a negligible share of denials.
claims.evidence: The median lender cites 'application incomplete' on 2.8% of denials, but one large lender cites it on 75.2% (Carrington Mortgage Services LLC). Negligible at the median, dominant at one door.

claims.claim: A low denial rate means a lender is easy to get approved with.
claims.evidence: A low observed rate can mean lenient underwriting, or an applicant mix that arrives pre-screened, or buyers steered away before filing. The record contains none of the three; only observed rates.
claims.note: Boundary: HMDA has no credit scores and no record of applications never filed.

claims.claim: FHA is easier to get than a conventional mortgage.
claims.evidence: This dataset is FHA only (loan_type 2). No conventional comparison is published here, and the two programs draw different applicants, so a raw comparison would not answer the question anyway.

claims.claim: The denial rate is the same for a buyer regardless of where they live.
claims.evidence: State-level 2025 rates differ substantially; the small-loan penalty alone ranges 1.19x to 4.45x by jurisdiction. Geography is a variable the record can see.

claims.claim: Your credit score is the single most important factor in an FHA denial.
claims.evidence: HMDA does not contain credit scores. The record can show that debt-to-income is the most-cited reason, but it cannot rank score against anything, so this belief cannot be confirmed or refuted from the public data.
claims.note: The most common belief about denials is one the public record is structurally unable to test.

claims.claim: Refinance applications are denied about as often as purchase applications.
claims.evidence: Loan-purpose splits are not among this project's published figures for 2025; the 2023 purchase-only vs refinance figures circulating online come from another universe and vintage.

claims.claim: A lender with a high denial rate is doing something wrong.
claims.evidence: An observed rate carries no information about conduct. High rates are screening signals about institutions, consistent with strict underwriting, a hard applicant mix, or filing practice; the record cannot distinguish them.
claims.note: This is the boundary every figure on the site carries.

claims.claim: Most FHA applications that reach a decision are approved.
claims.evidence: 77.9% of decisioned 2025 FHA applications were not denied (925,356 of 1,187,606).

claims.claim: Debt-to-income is one of the main reasons FHA applications are denied.
claims.evidence: It is the reason with the highest median share across the 95 of the 100 largest lenders that report reasons: 40.8%.

claims.claim: FHA lending is concentrated in a relatively small number of large lenders.
claims.evidence: The 100 largest FHA lenders accounted for about 78% of all decisioned FHA applications in 2025 (928,266 of 1,187,606, counting the 98 with published files).

claims.claim: A lender's strictness is the same for every kind of loan it makes.
claims.evidence: This project publishes conditional maps per lender (strictness by loan size and leverage cell) for some lenders, but a general test across all lenders is not published; treated as untestable in this battery.
